column3: It closely repeats the permission for livestock with the exception of what is recited, while framing it by binding obligations.
Its call to heed a reminder does not clarify sacred limits, permitted livestock, idolatry, or false speech.
It distinguishes originally lawful food from a self-imposed prohibition and calls for verification, extending the focus's lawful-excepted pattern.
The adjacent ayah directly identifies honoring God's ritual symbols with piety of the heart.
It joins rites, God's name over bestowed livestock, exclusive divinity, and submission, directly expanding the focus's ritual setting.
It shows that wholesome things once permitted can become prohibited as a consequence of wrongdoing and obstruction.
It explicitly calls idolatrous cult objects filth and commands believers to avoid them.
Created signs in heaven and earth provide only a broad setting for God-consciousness.
Its universal summons to worship God and avoid false authorities directly parallels the focus's rejection of idols.
It details forbidden foods and sacrifices made at idolatrous altars, directly specifying both exceptions and idolatrous practice.
Its warning against leading others from God's way is a local contrast to honoring His limits.
Abraham's prayer to be kept from worshipping idols gives a direct personal form of the commanded avoidance.
It exposes invented restrictions on livestock and false claims about God, directly countering both themes in the focus.
The command to come in submission adds only a general posture of yielding.
Visiting graves does not clarify the focus's limits, permissions, or prohibitions.
God's distinction between permitted trade and forbidden usury provides a separate example of divinely drawn legal limits.
Its assigned rites for every community extend the local ritual framework, though less directly than the livestock passage.
It directly commends those who neither witness falsehood nor engage vain speech.
It identifies livestock as a divine provision for riding and eating, adding their ordinary permitted use.
The question about renewed creation does not add to the focus's stated concerns.
The claim of being deprived has no useful connection to sacred limits or avoidance.
It uses filth for the condition placed on those who refuse understanding, offering a secondary contrast to idolatrous filth.
The reward of believers and good works is a general local consequence without the focus's specific relations.
The right of the needy does not clarify the focus.
Its rulings on women and orphans do not add to the focus's themes.
Praise before sunrise and sunset gives only a general worship response amid hostile speech.
The pious being kept away from the Fire supplies only a secondary image of protective avoidance.
Fasting concessions and feeding do not clarify the focus's sacred limits or idols.
The warning about blind hearts provides a local account of failed receptivity, not the focus's commands.
Its prayer and purification restrictions offer a distant example of regulated worship and speech awareness.
It permits eating from livestock God provided while forbidding the following of Satan's steps.
It calls unauthorized idol-names filth and challenges their claimed authority, reinforcing the rejection of idols.
Its detailed personal permissions are only a distant example of bounded lawful allowance.
The claim that revelation is merely human speech is a limited instance of a corrupt utterance.
The ruined towns and abandoned well do not clarify the focus's commands.
It pairs avoiding the worship of false authorities with turning back to God.
Its family-marriage prohibitions provide only a general example of legal boundaries.
Punishment for sins and sealed hearts are a broad warning rather than a direct counterpart.
It connects lawful wholesome provision with gratitude and worship of God.
Remembering recited verses and wisdom does not add a specific link.
The creation and resurrection signs do not clarify the focus's limits or prohibitions.
Its marriage restriction does not contribute to the focus's central themes.
Its prescribed worship and charitable duties give only a broad practical frame of obedience.
The command to praise and seek forgiveness offers only a general response to hostile words.
It explicitly calls divine limits boundaries not to be approached, giving a distinct practical account of honoring them.
Repentance for taking the calf gives a concrete consequence of idolatry.
The question about arrogant people does not clarify the focus.
Its permissions and restriction on hunting while consecrated show lawful allowance operating within a sacred state.
It condemns invoking another god without proof, directly supporting exclusive worship and rejection of idols.
The Fire's distant rage does not add to the focus's stated commands.
Avoiding major sins and indecencies gives a broader moral counterpart to the focus's command to avoid.
Belief on hearing revelation and prior submission offer only a general receptive response.
The list of earlier deniers does not clarify the focus.
It treats the sacred month and sacred mosque as weighty inviolabilities while condemning obstruction from God's way.
Purification from filth and commands to obey give a secondary purity-and-obedience parallel.
Entry into Paradise does not clarify the focus's limits or prohibitions.
Its personal marital restriction is a remote example of a defined lawful boundary.
The creation of pairs among livestock adds only a broad creation reference.
The invitation to the abode of peace and guidance has no specific link.
The wretched person's turning away from the reminder offers a contrary sense of avoidance.
Provision and spending do not clarify the focus's commands.
Moses' fear of being killed does not add to the focus.
It explicitly treats sacred months and inviolabilities as protected limits, even in reciprocal conflict.
Its mention of livestock pairs is secondary to its creation account.
The patient servants' reward does not clarify the focus.
Its protections in marriage and inheritance do not add to the focus's central relations.
The recited Book as mercy and reminder provides only a general connection to what is recited.
The named destroyed peoples do not clarify the focus.
It commands people to eat what is lawful and wholesome and not follow Satan.
Filth placed on unbelievers is only a secondary use of the focus's term.
It calls human life inviolable except by right, extending the idea of God-set sacred protections.
The accountability of every utterance makes speech morally consequential, complementing the ban on false speech.
It distinguishes avoidance of major sins and indecencies from lesser slips, refining the moral scope of avoidance.
Fear of the Lord and reward with Him provide only a general moral outcome.
It details what God has forbidden in food, permits necessity as an exception, and warns against desire without knowledge.
It explicitly characterizes a marital formula as objectionable and false speech.
Human turning away in ease gives only a broad contrast to grateful obedience.
Abraham and his followers disavow what others worship besides God, extending the focus's anti-idolatry stance.
Its reference to the inviolable city offers a distinct instance of a sacred protected domain.
The sun's course by the cave and the guidance statement do not clarify the focus.
The due share for the needy does not add to the focus.
The messenger's lack of requested payment does not clarify the focus.
Its ordered prohibitions begin with not associating anything with God, strongly expanding the focus's protected moral limits.
It joins worship of idols with fabricating falsehood and redirects worship and provision to God alone.
It rebukes making forbidden what God has made lawful, directly illuminating the focus's distinction between permission and prohibition.
It portrays idol-devotion as a worldly bond that collapses into mutual rejection and punishment.
Lawful wholesome provision with God-consciousness repeats the permission theme after closer parallels.
Despair of God's mercy does not clarify the focus.
The secure sanctuary supplies a concrete instance of a God-given inviolable protected space.
A good word and forgiveness offer only a broad ethical counterpart to the command against false speech.
Its divorce regulation does not add to the focus's central relations.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the focus.
Ignorance of God's revealed limits supplies only a general contrast to honoring them.
Noah's summons to worship God alone gives a general but direct anti-idolatry counterpart.
It rejects a false claim about God and states that all in heaven and earth are devoutly obedient to Him.
A town's beneficial faith and removal of disgrace provide only a broad consequence of belief.
The angels' fearful concern before God gives only a general posture of reverence.
Turning away when called to God's Book gives a general contrary response to divinely set judgment.
The exception of those who pray gives only a minimal worship connection.
Guidance to the straight path does not add a specific link to the focus.
It establishes the House as a purified place of worship, giving a concrete setting for honoring God's sacred ordinances.
It supplies the food prohibitions and necessity exception that illuminate the focus's permitted-livestock clause.
Completing pilgrimage and offering sacrificial animals develops the ritual obligations surrounding the sacred precinct.
Its prohibitions during pilgrimage give a practical account of conduct within a consecrated observance.
The first House established for worship provides a foundational sacred-place context.
The inviolable House and pilgrimage duty further specify reverence for God's sacred institutions.
Its statement that associating partners with God is not forgiven directly reinforces the gravity of the focus's anti-idolatry command.
It explicitly commands believers not to violate God's symbols, sacred months, offerings, or garlanded animals.
It pairs lawful good things with invoking God's name over trained hunting animals, closely extending the focus's food-and-ritual rule.
The permission of wholesome food adds a distinct legal expression of divinely allowed provision.
It forbids believers from making unlawful the good things God has made lawful and commands them not to transgress.
Its hunting prohibition and expiation while consecrated show how sacred status regulates otherwise permitted animals.
It names the Kaaba, sacred month, offerings, and garlands as divinely established sacred markers.
It rejects invented livestock taboos and attributes their fabrication to disbelief about God.
It commands eating from that over which God's name has been mentioned, directly complementing the livestock exception.
It forbids eating what lacks God's name and calls it defiance, directly clarifying the focus's food boundary.
It exposes polytheists' false allocations of crops and livestock between God and their associates.
Its accounting of livestock pairs challenges unsupported claims about what God has forbidden.
It lists the revealed food prohibitions and their exception, directly specifying the focus's recited exclusions.
It joins prohibited indecencies, injustice, associating partners with God, and speaking about God without knowledge.
It connects polytheism with impurity and protection of the Sacred Mosque.
Its sacred-month order and warning against self-wronging extend the category of divinely protected times.
It rejects worship of beings besides God and the unsupported claims made for their intercession.
It rebukes people for declaring parts of God's provision lawful and forbidden without warrant.
It repeats the specific food prohibitions and necessity exception that frame what remains permitted.
It directly forbids saying falsely that something is lawful or forbidden in order to fabricate a lie about God.
The Sacred Mosque and its surrounding blessed precinct provide a distinct sacred-place context.
It forbids following what one has no knowledge of, placing a limit on unsupported assertion.
It safeguards access to the Sacred Mosque and threatens those who seek wrongful deviation within it.
It commands Abraham to purify the House and not associate anything with God, joining sacred space with exclusive worship.
It has pilgrims name God over the livestock He provided, then eat and feed others, directly expanding the focus's ritual provision.
It commands pilgrims to complete their rites and vows and circumambulate the Ancient House.
It immediately specifies turning wholly to God without associating partners with Him.
It identifies appointed benefits in sacrificial animals before their destination at the Ancient House.
It makes sacrificial camels among God's symbols and commands His name over them before eating and feeding others.
It states that neither meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does, clarifying the inward purpose of sacrificial observance.
It condemns passing a false report from tongue to tongue and speaking without knowledge.
It explicitly says that repeating such a falsehood is not fitting and calls it a grave matter.
It commands God-consciousness and straight, sound speech, giving the positive counterpart to avoiding false utterance.
It affirms pure religion for God and challenges taking protectors besides Him.
It warns that associating partners with God nullifies works, sharpening the focus's anti-idolatry boundary.
It requires verification of a corrupt person's report, providing a practical safeguard against false speech.
It names the idols al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, providing a concrete idolatry context.
It rejects idol names as unsupported conjecture, closely connecting false naming with false worship.
It declares that places of worship belong to God alone and forbids calling upon anyone alongside Him.
